    Expand Full Lineage & Technical Proof

    Given-When-Then Acceptance Criteria

    Scenario 1 — Session attendance beyond capacity flagged

    Given a Session has a confirmed venue booking When its expected attendance changes Then each booking whose own headcount is set uses that headcount, otherwise it uses the Session attendance; only a booking whose governing headcount exceeds capacity is flagged and Venue Staff are notified

    Scenario 2 — Description-only edit flags nothing

    Given an Event has confirmed venue and equipment arrangements When only its Event description is edited Then no arrangements are flagged

    Scenario 3 — Affected Session arrangements shown first

    Given a change affects confirmed arrangements When I save it Then I am shown the affected Session bookings, equipment reservations and staffed Technical Support requests before the change takes effect (T-104)

    Scenario 4 — Over-subscription warns only

    Given a change would make a Session or combined Event registration capacity lower than approved registrations When the change is saved Then I am warned and shown the over-subscription, and no Attendee is automatically removed or waitlisted

    Scenario 5 — Session date/time change flags its arrangements

    Given a Session date or time changes When the change takes effect Then that Session's venue booking and equipment reservations, and any staffed Technical Support request overlapping its previous time, are flagged for reconfirmation; an Event-wide date/time change flags all of its Session arrangements and every staffed Technical Support request; a flagged Technical Support request counts as outstanding for readiness until Technical Support Staff reconfirm it at the new time (T-104)

    Scenario 6 — Affected staff notified

    Given a change flags a venue, equipment or Technical Support staffing arrangement When the affected arrangements are identified Then the assigned Venue Staff and Technical Support Staff are notified

    Definition of Done Verification Checklist (7 criteria)

    • ☑ Flag only the Session arrangement whose governing headcount exceeds capacity
    • ☑ Leave arrangements unflagged for description-only edits
    • ☑ Show affected Session bookings/reservations before applying a change
    • ☑ Warn about over-subscription without automatically removing or waitlisting Attendees
    • ☑ Flag the affected Session or all Sessions for date/time changes as appropriate
    • ☑ Flag staffed Technical Support requests on a date/time change and let Technical Support Staff reconfirm them at the new time (T-104)
    • ☑ Notify staff responsible for the affected arrangements

    Handle a venue lost from a confirmed event

    SAY THIS FIRST (10-SEC HOOK)

    "Handles venue loss when venue becomes unavailable: booking is marked Conflicting, event returns to Planning, original details preserved (T-81)."

    Known Limitation / Boundary: Coordinator searches replacement; lifting block does not overwrite active replacement (PR #355 / PR #367 fix).
    BDR Lineage:
    C-66 ConnectSphere needs Venue Staff to be able to mark a venue temporarily unavailable because of maintenance, equipment failure, renovation, safety concerns, or other operational reasons. This may occur even when future events have already been booked at the venue. When this happens, the existing event itself should not automatically be cancelled. Instead, affected bookings should be identified and the relevant Event Coordinators informed that alternative arrangements are required. The system should preserve the original event information while allowing the coordinator to search for and request a replacement venue. C-61 Venue Staff update venue availability when operational changes occur, triggering a notification to the Event Coordinator to re-evaluate arrangements. While the event status remains visible, the system notifies relevant stakeholders of the venue issue so the coordinator can initiate changes. The co-ordinator will contact the Organiser, liaise about the changes offline and reach an agreement with the organiser. Subsequently the co-ordinator will make relevant changes to the event according to the agreement. C-120 Should revert to Planning review. The event itself is preserve and not automatically cancelled. Affected Coordinators are notified to find replacement venues, reverting the status to planning/change review. C-121 The Event Coordinator is informed immediately to arrange alternative venues working with the organiser; Organisers and Attendees are notified when replacement arrangements or formal event changes are confirmed. T-28 The Coordinator may revert Confirmed to Planning T-67 Deliver Change 2 as a new E05 story that withdraws E05-S04's refusal of blocks over confirmed bookings, and return E10-S05 to Release 1 T-73 Write the Week 7 stories now against recorded defaults and amend after the customer Q&A, rather than waiting T-74 A Done story stays Done; new behaviour that touches it is a new story; an incomplete story is updated in place; a story is reopened only when one of its original criteria turns out unsatisfied T-81 A venue loss returns a Confirmed event to Planning and notifies its Coordinator O-24 O-25
    Architectural Decisions:
    ADR-017 Story owners build their own frontend on a shared skeleton

    Expand Full Lineage & Technical Proof

    Given-When-Then Acceptance Criteria

    Scenario 1 — Lost venue flags the event

    Given my event has a Pending or Confirmed venue booking When Venue Staff mark that venue unavailable over the booking's period (E05-S06) Then I am notified, the booking shows as Conflicting on the event, and the event is flagged as needing alternative arrangements; a Confirmed event returns to Planning without being cancelled, and every other arrangement stays as it was (C-120, T-81)

    Scenario 2 — Flagged event offers a replacement search

    Given my event is flagged When I open it Then the reason category, the period and the affected booking are shown, the original venue, dates and requirements are preserved, and I can start a venue search (E06-S01) for the same event from that screen

    Scenario 3 — Replacement requested without losing the original

    Given I have found a replacement venue When I submit a booking request for it (E06-S03) Then the request is created for the same event alongside the Conflicting booking, and I may cancel the Conflicting booking explicitly once the replacement is Confirmed; nothing is cancelled for me

    Scenario 4 — Organiser and Attendees told on the actual change

    Given my event lost its venue When the replacement booking is confirmed Then the Organiser and registered Attendees are notified of the new venue through the existing venue-change routing (E11-S01), and not earlier (C-121, T-81)

    Definition of Done Verification Checklist (5 criteria)

    • ☑ Be notified when a venue I have booked is marked unavailable over my booking, and see a Confirmed event return to Planning without being cancelled
    • ☑ See the reason, period and affected booking on the event, with the original event information intact
    • ☑ Start a venue search for the same event from the flagged event
    • ☑ Request a replacement venue while the Conflicting booking remains on the event until I cancel it
    • ☑ Confirm the Organiser and registered Attendees are told of the venue change only when it actually happens

    Technical Slice Architecture

    Route / Endpoint: GET /api/venues/recovery?event=<id>, POST /api/venues/recovery?action=replace
    Backend Controller: backend/src/modules/venueBooking/lostVenueRecovery.ts
    Database Migration: 0025_venue_unavailability.sql

    Notify users about events they are involved in

    SAY THIS FIRST (10-SEC HOOK)

    "Transactional notification hub: inserts in-app notices and email outbox entries inside the business SQL transaction (T-37/T-105 XXL=13pts)."

    Known Limitation / Boundary: Outbox pattern guarantees zero orphaned emails if business transaction rolls back; Brevo external relay processes asynchronously.
    BDR Lineage:
    C-04 Delivery channel choice is flexible and up to your team's implementation (in-app or external channels). C-29 System notifications are required for major events, but user notification preferences/toggles are left to implementation design. C-53 Notifications reach relevant roles (coordinators get operational updates; organisers get status changes). Specific routing per notification is flexible. C-68 Venue Staff have explained that they sometimes temporarily hold a venue while an Event Coordinator is finalising event arrangements. These tentative holds should not reserve a venue indefinitely. Each hold must therefore have an expiry date/time. If the required action is not completed before the deadline, the hold should expire and the venue should become available for other requests. The Event Coordinator should be informed before or when the hold expires, and an expired hold should not be treated as a confirmed booking. C-69 ConnectSphere has introduced a new internal role, the Event Coordinator Lead, who is responsible for overseeing incoming event requests and assigning them to individual Event Coordinators. Newly submitted event requests should no longer be assigned directly to an Event Coordinator. Instead, they first enter an unassigned queue that can be viewed by the Event Coordinator Lead. The Lead can review basic event information, assign a suitable Event Coordinator, and reassign events where necessary. Event Coordinators should only be able to manage events assigned to them, while the Event Coordinator Lead should be able to view all coordinator assignments and active events under their supervision. Relevant users should be notified when assignments or reassignments occur. C-79 The Venue Staff specify the expiry date/time per hold based on their knowledge. System notifies/warns the Coordinator before or when the hold expires. The warning time can be set by the coordinator per event hold. C-99 Venue Staff specify the expiry date/time per hold based on venue knowledge; length is not fixed by the system. C-124 Venue Staff set/update the expiry date/time per hold based on venue knowledge. C-125 Week 7 Changes.docx requires informing the Event Coordinator before or when the hold expires via notifications. C-128 Assignment and reassignment by the Lead take effect immediately in the system with notifications sent to relevant users. C-129 All coordinator assignments and reassignments are managed by the Event Coordinator Lead, the system do not manage the reassignment request T-35 Notifications delivered in-app and by email T-36 Schedule notifications in Sprint 2 as an enabler T-44 Merge the two notification stories into one E11-S01 T-48 Withdraw the sessions model T-64 Approve E11-S01 recipient routing and incremental transactional integration T-69 Amend T-49: every tentative hold carries an expiry and is expired by the system T-70 Retire T-14 and rewrite E03-S01 around an unassigned queue worked by the Event Coordinator Lead C-70 ConnectSphere has introduced a new internal role, the Safety Officer, who is responsible for reviewing the operational safety of planned events. After the venue and technical arrangements have been confirmed, the Safety Officer must conduct an Operational Safety Check before the event can proceed to preparation. The review considers factors such as expected attendance, venue capacity and layout, emergency access, accessibility requirements, equipment placement, crowd movement, and any known venue restrictions. The Safety Officer may approve the event, reject the safety arrangement, or request changes. If changes are required, the event returns to the relevant earlier planning stage and affected venue or technical arrangements may need to be reviewed again. The event cannot proceed to preparation until the Safety Officer has approved it. You can assume that the Safety Officer will always give a response (approve/reject/request). T-71 Add a Safety Review gate between Planning and Confirmed as the interim placement of C-70's Operational Safety Check
    Architectural Decisions:
    ADR-006 Transactional outbox for notification delivery

    TC_E11S01_08 — Verify that email provider failure does not affect the business change or the in-app notification
    Negative Guardrail / Business Rule (IS212 Step 4)

    Scenario: Verify that email provider failure does not affect the business change or the in

    🎙️ Why We Chose This Test (Spoken Defense):

    Validates defensive exception handling and business rule enforcement. As emphasized in IS212 Week 4 Slide 26 and Week 6, this test proves the system rejects invalid inputs or unauthorized operations with predictable error responses (HTTP 4xx), protecting database consistency (E11-S01 · Scenario 4 (Delivered in-app and by email) · ADR-006).

    💥 What Would Have to Be Broken to Fail (First Principles):

    Atomic insert into notification_outbox table, background relay daemon polling, or recipient email template rendering.

    Pre-conditions: Synthetic Event EVT-2003 has an assigned Coordinator and a pending venue booking in a disposable local PostgreSQL database. The test harness controls the HTTP email provider response; no live provider credentials, production endpoint changes or real mailbox sends are used. Prepare explicit rejection and ambiguous transport-outcome variants separately.

    Steps: 1. As responsible Venue Staff, approve the pending venue booking for EVT-2003 through the real booking workflow. 2. Confirm the booking is Confirmed and the assigned Coordinator has its in-app notification before dispatching the email. 3. For the explicit-rejection variant, dispatch the committed email using a controlled HTTP 400/401 provider response and inspect its delivery state and sanitized reason. 4. On a separate synthetic change, simulate a lost response/network timeout or HTTP 503. Inspect both delivery_status and dispatch_state; retry dispatch and verify that an uncertain outcome is retained without a second provider call. 5. Re-read each booking and Coordinator inbox. The committed business state and in-app notice must remain intact in both variants.

    Expected outcome: The booking remains Confirmed and the Coordinator's in-app notification persists; later email failure never rolls back the business transaction. Explicit rejection records delivery_status=failed and dispatch_state=failed with sanitized provider_rejected. An ambiguous outcome records delivery_status=failed and dispatch_state=uncertain with provider_outcome_unknown, retaining its prepared content and refusing automatic resend; do not claim that the provider definitely did not accept that email. HTTP 429 uses bounded retry and does not change the committed business state. These controlled-provider results do not prove actual registered-mailbox delivery, which remains TC_E11S01_05.

    Justification: Acceptance scenario and expected result define the reason for this case.

    TC_E11S01_15 — Deduplicate concurrent notification-hook retries
    Integration & State Integrity (IS212 Week 9)

    Scenario: Deduplicate concurrent notification-hook retries

    🎙️ Why We Chose This Test (Spoken Defense):

    Tests cross-boundary persistence and relational cascades against real PostgreSQL (avoiding the 'mock-based integration illusion', Week 9 Slide 20). Verifies rollback semantics under failure for E11-S01 - approved routing extension (T-64); ADR-006.

    💥 What Would Have to Be Broken to Fail (First Principles):

    Atomic insert into notification_outbox table, background relay daemon polling, or recipient email template rendering.

    Pre-conditions: Two transactions use the same event, stable change ID and recipient snapshot.

    Steps: 1. Call the notification hook concurrently and commit both attempts.

    Expected outcome: Exactly one in-app row and one email-delivery row exist per recipient for the logical change. A new change ID identifies a different business change.

    Justification: Acceptance scenario and expected result define the reason for this case.

    TC_E11S01_16 — Keep uncommitted notifications invisible and roll back all writes
    Integration & State Integrity (IS212 Week 9)

    Scenario: Keep uncommitted notifications invisible and roll back all writes

    🎙️ Why We Chose This Test (Spoken Defense):

    Tests cross-boundary persistence and relational cascades against real PostgreSQL (avoiding the 'mock-based integration illusion', Week 9 Slide 20). Verifies rollback semantics under failure for E11-S01 - approved routing extension (T-64); ADR-006.

    💥 What Would Have to Be Broken to Fail (First Principles):

    Atomic insert into notification_outbox table, background relay daemon polling, or recipient email template rendering.

    Pre-conditions: A business transaction has inserted notifications and prepared email delivery rows but has not committed.

    Steps: 1. Read from another connection, then force the business transaction to roll back.

    Expected outcome: The other connection cannot observe the uncommitted messages. After rollback no notification or email-delivery row remains.

    Justification: Acceptance scenario and expected result define the reason for this case.

    Expand Full Lineage & Technical Proof

    Given-When-Then Acceptance Criteria

    Scenario 1 — Status change notified

    Given I am a recipient under the approved routing matrix When an event status changes or a booking decision is made Then I receive a notification stating what changed, when, and which event it concerns, unless I performed the action myself

    Scenario 2 — All affected parties notified

    Given the event's date, time or venue changes When the change takes effect Then the Event Organiser, assigned Event Coordinator, affected assigned Venue Staff, affected assigned Technical Support Staff, registered Attendees and waitlisted Attendees are notified according to the routing matrix, excluding the acting user

    Scenario 3 — Unaffected users not notified

    Given a change does not affect a particular user's responsibilities When the change occurs Then that user is not notified

    Scenario 4 — Delivered in-app and by email

    Given a notification is generated for me When it is delivered Then it appears in the system and is also sent to my registered email address

    Scenario 5 — Unread notifications distinguished

    Given I have several unread notifications When I open my notification list Then they are shown newest first with unread ones distinguished

    Scenario 6 — Marked as read

    Given I open an unread notification When I have read it Then it is marked as read

    Definition of Done Verification Checklist (11 criteria)

    • ☑ Receive a notification when an event I am linked to changes status
    • ☑ Receive a notification when a booking decision is made
    • ☑ Confirm all affected parties are notified when the event's date, time or venue changes
    • ☑ Confirm unaffected, inactive, withdrawn and unrelated users are not notified
    • ☑ Confirm the acting user is excluded and each recipient gets one notification per logical change
    • ☑ Confirm cancellation preserves recipients before links are released
    • ☑ Confirm internal booking decisions do not reach Attendees
    • ☑ See what changed, when, and which event and event it concerns
    • ☑ Receive the same notification in the system and by email
    • ☑ See notifications newest first with unread ones distinguished
    • ☑ Mark a notification as read

    💥 What Would Have to Be Broken to Fail (First Principles):

    Append-only audit_logs trigger, actor attribution context binding, or immutable log write constraint.

    Pre-conditions: Request "Annual Tech Summit" has status "Under Review"; coordinator_1@connectsphere.com is an Event Coordinator permitted to view and approve it

    Steps: 1. As coordinator_1@connectsphere.com, approve the request (status -> Approved) 2. Open the approved event's existing detail page as that Coordinator 3. Locate the status-change entry in its Activity log 4. Compare the displayed actor, action and timestamp with the completed change and affected event

    Expected outcome: An entry is recorded with actor = coordinator_1@connectsphere.com, action = "Status changed to Approved", event = Annual Tech Summit, and a timestamp; the Event Coordinator can read it on that event under existing access rules, without an Administrator role or global audit screen

    Justification: Acceptance scenario and expected result define the reason for this case.

    TC_E14S02_05 — Verify that any attempt to edit or delete an activity log entry should be refused
    Negative Guardrail / Business Rule (IS212 Step 4)

    Scenario: Verify that any attempt to edit or delete an activity log entry should be refuse

    🎙️ Why We Chose This Test (Spoken Defense):

    Validates defensive exception handling and business rule enforcement. As emphasized in IS212 Week 4 Slide 26 and Week 6, this test proves the system rejects invalid inputs or unauthorized operations with predictable error responses (HTTP 4xx), protecting database consistency (E14-S02 - Scenario 5 (Log entries immutable; T-75, T-76)).

    💥 What Would Have to Be Broken to Fail (First Principles):

    Append-only audit_logs trigger, actor attribution context binding, or immutable log write constraint.

    Pre-conditions: A log entry exists: Event = Annual Tech Summit, Action = "Status changed to Approved", Actor = coordinator_1@connectsphere.com (created in TC_E14S02_01 or an equivalent independent fixture in a disposable test database)

    Steps: 1. As an Event Coordinator permitted to view the event, open its Activity log 2. Confirm no edit or delete control is offered for the entry 3. For each existing application role (event_organiser, event_coordinator, venue_staff, technical_support_staff and attendee), attempt direct API update and delete requests against the entry 4. As the database test harness, attempt UPDATE and DELETE of that entry through the application database connection in separate transactions 5. Read the original entry after each refused attempt to confirm its contents and row remain unchanged

    Expected outcome: All update and delete attempts are refused. Unsupported API methods or routes may return 404/405; protected mutation routes must reject unauthorised requests. No response may represent a successful mutation. The database rejects both operations and the entry remains unchanged. No Administrator role is required.

    Justification: Acceptance scenario and expected result define the reason for this case.

    Given-When-Then Acceptance Criteria

    Scenario 1 — Both existing readers see Singapore time

    Given an authorised Organiser or assigned Coordinator opens the existing event Activity log When an entry displays an edited date/time field value Then each date/time value already displayed by that view uses the existing shared Singapore formatter, including both old and new values where already shown, independently of the browser timezone; 2026-10-15T09:30:00Z represents 15 October 2026 at 17:30 Singapore time, not 16 October. Existing field keys are startAt, endAt and registrationDates; registrationDates stores "opensAt to closesAt", so both endpoints are formatted for display without changing that stored string.

    Scenario 2 — Singapore calendar rollover

    Given an edited date/time value is 2026-10-15T18:30:00Z When either view displays it Then it represents 16 October 2026 at 02:30 Singapore time; the calendar date as well as the hour is converted correctly.

    Scenario 3 — Missing and invalid values keep the existing contract

    Given a date/time value is missing or invalid When formatting is needed Then formatDate retains its existing "Not recorded" result; each view retains its existing omission/label-only behavior for absent change values, without throwing, inventing a date or introducing a new fallback.

    Scenario 4 — Other values and existing display paths unchanged

    Given an entry contains ordinary text, a status change or a venue hold expiry When either view renders it Then ordinary text remains text, existing status labels/badges remain unchanged, and existing hold-expiry formatting and behavior are preserved; the correction is field-aware, not conversion of every date-looking string.

    Scenario 5 — Audit evidence and access unchanged

    Given the existing event access rules apply When either permitted reader views or reloads the formatted log Then stored UTC old_value/new_value and occurred_at, actor and action remain unchanged and immutable; unauthorised readers remain refused and access-denial entries remain hidden from event logs, with no new audit viewer or permissions.

    Definition of Done Verification Checklist (5 criteria)

    • ☑ Scope implementation to the edited date/time value rendering in frontend/src/features/organiser/ClientEvents.tsx and frontend/src/features/events/ActivityLog.tsx using shared formatDate
    • ☑ Cover both views, same-day and rollover boundaries, missing/invalid inputs, other values and immutable/access-preserving reads with TC_E14S03_01 to _06
    • ☑ Do not add before/after history to a view that does not already show it; wider E14-S01 history remains separate
    • ☑ Exclude notification "Changed at ...Z" text, unrelated action/field labels, global viewers, new notifications and changes to stored audit data or hold-expiry behavior
    • ☑ Obtain human code/test review and future T-65/T-93 manual evidence; these planned cases are not execution evidence

    19 Architecture Decision Records (ADR-001 to ADR-019)

    ADR-001

    Modular monolith rather than microservices

    Accepted
    Related BDR: C-03 C-13 C-39 T-24

    Context

    The hardest requirements in this system are transactional. E06-S06 must prevent a venue being committed to two events. E09-S02 must handle two Attendees claiming the final place simultaneously. E07-S04 must stop the same equipment being reserved for overlapping sessions. §8d requires that users never see contradictory information about dates, bookings, equipment or registration status. Against that, §8e asks for three years of growth for a regional operator with roughly 500 staff, and §8g asks that new functionality and business rules can be added without rebuilding the system. The team is a group of students working across four sprints.

    Decision

    A single deployable application server containing all domain components, backed by one PostgreSQL database, plus two background processes for notification delivery (see ADR-006). Component boundaries are maintained in the codebase but not across the network.

    Alternatives Considered

    - Microservices per bounded context (venue, equipment, registration). Rejected because conflict detection and capacity enforcement span those contexts. Registration must read the booked venue's capacity; confirmation must read the event's venue and equipment state. Splitting them means distributed transactions or sagas with compensating actions, and it makes ADR-003 impossible. - Serverless functions. Rejected because connection pooling against a relational database and cold-start latency both work against §8a.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    📄 View ADR-001-modular-monolith-rather-than-microservices.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-002

    PostgreSQL as the system of record

    Accepted
    Related BDR: C-27

    Context

    Almost every scarce resource in this system is booked over a time interval: venues, equipment quantities, and technical staff. §8d requires consistency across related arrangements and §8f requires an audit trail of what changed, who changed it and when.

    Decision

    PostgreSQL 16, using tstzrange for every time interval, with the btree_gist extension enabled.

    Alternatives Considered

    - MySQL. Rejected because it has no native range type and no exclusion constraints, so all overlap detection falls back to application logic. - A document store. Rejected because overlap queries are awkward and the multi-entity consistency §8d requires would have to be built by hand. - Separate start_time and end_time columns. Rejected because overlap predicates then need four comparisons and are easy to get wrong at the boundaries, particularly around inclusive versus exclusive endpoints.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    📄 View ADR-002-postgresql-as-the-system-of-record.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-003

    Enforce booking and assignment conflicts in the database

    Accepted
    Related BDR: C-01 C-16 C-37 C-46 C-65 C-67 C-68 T-66 T-68 T-69

    Context

    E06-S06 Scenario 3 states that when another Venue Staff member approves a conflicting request moments earlier, the second approval must fail and the approver must be told the venue has just been taken. E07-S07 states a colleague cannot hold two overlapping assignments. A check-then-insert in application code has a race window: two concurrent approvals can both read the venue as free before either writes.

    Decision

    Exclusion constraints in the database: ALTER TABLE venue_bookings ADD CONSTRAINT no_double_booking EXCLUDE USING gist (venue_id WITH =, booking_range WITH &&) WHERE (status = 'confirmed'); ALTER TABLE tech_staff_assignments ADD CONSTRAINT no_staff_overlap EXCLUDE USING gist (staff_id WITH =, assignment_range WITH &&) WHERE (status = 'active');

    Alternatives Considered

    - Application-level check before insert. Rejected: this is precisely the race E06-S06 Scenario 3 describes, and no amount of care in application code closes it. - Pessimistic locking with SELECT FOR UPDATE. Correct, but requires every code path touching bookings to take the lock in the right order. One missed path reopens the hole. - SERIALIZABLE isolation. Correct, but raises abort rates across all transactions and pushes retry logic into every caller.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    📄 View ADR-003-enforce-booking-and-assignment-conflicts-in-the-database.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-004

    Sessions as a first-class entity — RETIRED

    RETIRED — superseded in version 3 by C-62 and T-48
    Related BDR: C-19 C-62 T-19 T-21 T-48

    Context

    Week 1 §4 describes Multi-Session Events, where sessions may fall on the same day or across several days with different timings and operational requirements. Bryan (G1) confirmed per-session operational requirements exist, while noting that automatic session-by-session venue splitting rules have not been discussed.

    Decision

    An event comprises one or more sessions. Venue bookings, equipment requests and reservations, technical support requests and attendee registrations all attach to a session. A single-session event is the common case and requires no additional structure from the user.

    Alternatives Considered

    - Event-level scheduling with one start and end time. Rejected: it cannot express a three-day conference whose second day needs a different room, different equipment and a different expected attendance. - A separate sub-event entity with a parent link. Rejected: it duplicates the entire event lifecycle, and confirmation and status would then have to be reconciled between parent and children.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    📄 View ADR-004-sessions-as-a-first-class-entity-retired.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-005

    Denormalise event_id, guarded by a composite foreign key — RETIRED

    RETIRED — superseded in version 3 by C-62 and T-48
    Related BDR: T-21 C-62 T-48

    Context

    Following ADR-004, bookings, reservations and registrations belong to a session. But the most frequent queries are event-scoped: listing everything for an event, and the authorisation check that runs on every Organiser request.

    Decision

    Session-scoped tables carry both session_id and event_id. SESSIONS gains UNIQUE (id, event_id), and the dependent tables reference that pair as a composite foreign key.

    Alternatives Considered

    - Strict normalisation, session_id only. Rejected: every event-scoped query needs an extra join, including the authorisation check on the hot path. - Denormalise without the composite key. Rejected: nothing would prevent a booking pointing at session X and event Y where X does not belong to Y. That is silent data corruption, and it would surface as a confusing authorisation bug long after the write.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    📄 View ADR-005-denormalise-event-id-guarded-by-a-composite-foreign-key-retired.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-006

    Transactional outbox for notification delivery

    Accepted (amended 3 October 2026, see end)
    Related BDR: C-04 C-53 T-35 T-36 T-44 T-64

    Context

    E11-S01 requires notifications delivered both in-app and by email, and Charles (G2) confirmed the channel is the team's choice. Roughly fifteen stories across the release end an acceptance criterion with “and the Coordinator is notified”. §8a requires common operations to complete within a reasonable time, and the team has since set that at three seconds (BDR T-51). A notification must never be sent for a business change that did not commit. If a venue approval is rolled back after its notification has been queued, the Coordinator is told about a booking that does not exist.

    Decision

    The application server writes the business change and its notification delivery rows to PostgreSQL in a single transaction. A relay process polls the database for committed delivery rows with status queued and publishes one job per row to Redis. A worker process consumes jobs from Redis, calls the email provider, and records the outcome against the delivery row. The application never writes to Redis directly. Only committed rows are ever published.

    Alternatives Considered

    - Send email synchronously within the request. Rejected: an SMTP timeout would fail a venue approval that had otherwise succeeded, and every write would carry the email provider's latency against a three-second target. - Enqueue to Redis directly from the application immediately after writing to the database. This was the original design in version 1 of this record. Rejected because the enqueue sits outside the database transaction, so a rollback after enqueuing sends a notification for something that never happened. Version 1 recorded that risk as an accepted cost; the outbox removes it instead. - A database-polling job table with no Redis at all, the worker polling PostgreSQL directly. Genuinely simpler and one container fewer. Rejected because Redis provides retry, backoff and concurrent consumption without building them, and remains available as a cache. Note that the chosen design still polls the database: the two are not opposites. Polling carries the job out of the transaction boundary; Redis carries it to the worker.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    📄 View ADR-006-transactional-outbox-for-notification-delivery.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-007

    One single-page application for all roles (five, now seven)

    Accepted
    Related BDR: C-69 C-70 T-72

    Context

    Five roles use the system (§3), split between external and internal users. §7 requires the system to be both desktop- and mobile-friendly. §8c requires all groups to complete their common activities without extensive training.

    Decision

    A single React application with role-based navigation and views, rather than separate external and internal portals.

    Alternatives Considered

    - Separate external and internal applications. Rejected: it duplicates authentication, the event record display and the notification interface. An Organiser and a Coordinator look at largely the same event, differing in which fields are editable and which internal details are visible. - Server-rendered multi-page application. Rejected: the venue availability calendar and the search-and-filter screens are interaction-heavy enough that a full page load per interaction would work against §8c.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    📄 View ADR-007-one-single-page-application-for-all-five-roles.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-008

    Client organisation as the tenancy boundary

    Accepted
    Related BDR: C-40

    Context

    E01-S02 requires an Event Organiser to see only events belonging to their own client organisation, and §8b states an Organiser should not normally be able to view events belonging to unrelated clients. Week 1 §4 Client Management notes that several Organisers may belong to one organisation. Ewen (G1) confirmed Event Coordinators can see all events, so the restriction applies to Organisers rather than internal staff.

    Decision

    CLIENT_ORGANISATIONS is a first-class table. USERS and EVENTS both reference it. The Access Control component scopes every Organiser-facing query by client_org_id.

    Alternatives Considered

    - A free-text organisation name on the user record, as in the original draft. Rejected: two Organisers spelling the name differently land in two tenancies, and a name collision grants access across clients. This is a security property, not a data-tidiness one. - Schema- or database-per-tenant multi-tenancy. Rejected as far beyond the requirement. ConnectSphere owns all the data, and internal staff need visibility across clients.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    📄 View ADR-008-client-organisation-as-the-tenancy-boundary.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-009

    A single audit log with a polymorphic target

    Accepted
    Related BDR: T-04 C-70 T-71 T-75 T-76

    Context

    E14-S02 records event status changes, denied access attempts and account deactivations. E06-S04 owns venue booking approval, rejection and release logging after T-76 (2 October 2026). §8f requires ConnectSphere to determine what was changed, who changed it and when. Only the first of those four is always tied to an event.

    Decision

    One append-only AUDIT_LOGS table with entity_type, entity_id, and a nullable event_id carried denormalised for convenience. T-75 allows Event Coordinators to read the Activity log on events they are already permitted to view, through the existing event page. It adds no global audit permission or Administrator role. Denial and account-deactivation entries are inspected in a controlled test database for acceptance verification. Administrator viewing is deferred to Release 2. T-76 changes story ownership, not the shared append-only storage or the immutability requirement.

    Alternatives Considered

    - One table per log type. Rejected: §8f's single question would become a four-way UNION, and the immutability rule in E14-S02 would need enforcing in four places. - Logging only event-related actions. Rejected: denied access attempts and account deactivations are exactly the events an audit trail exists to capture.

    ADR-014

    One file per Vercel serverless API route

    Accepted
    Related BDR: T-56

    Context

    Every file under `api/` builds as one serverless function on Vercel. The URL a function serves is derived from its path: `api/foo.ts` serves `/api/foo`, and `api/foo/index.ts` also serves `/api/foo`. When both files exist the build succeeds without warning, both lambdas ship, and one silently wins the route while the other becomes unreachable. Empirically on the current builder the parent-level file wins, but Vercel does not document the tie-breaker, so the outcome is undefined by contract. This is not hypothetical. PR #56 (SCRUM-26 submit event request) added `api/events.ts` for the POST create path. `api/events/index.ts` already existed from PR #42 (SCRUM-18 hide internal planning info) serving the organiser browse-events GET listing. From the moment PR #56 shipped, `GET /api/events` in production returned `405 method_not_allowed` with `Allow: POST` — the organiser browse screen backed by `frontend/src/features/organiser/ClientEvents.tsx` was silently broken. Nobody noticed at review because the routing collision does not manifest in the build log, only at request time on the deployed URL, and the failing screen is behind SSO on the Vercel preview alias where teammates without dashboard access could not reach it. The Hobby plan compounds the failure mode. It caps a deployment at twelve serverless functions. Two colliding files consume two slots but only serve one route, so the collision costs a slot that a future story needs. On the deployment where this bug was discovered the project sat at exactly 12/12 functions with one of them dead, leaving zero headroom for the next feature.

    Decision

    Under `api/` every URL path is served by exactly one file. A multi-verb endpoint dispatches on `request.method` inside a single handler. A new endpoint either lives at a distinct file path or reuses an existing file via method dispatch. `api/foo/index.ts` is never allowed to coexist with `api/foo.ts`; either the folder holds only nested routes or the parent file is deleted. The file count under `api/` is kept at eleven or fewer as a soft limit. Twelve is the Hobby-plan hard cap; holding one slot in reserve means the next story never lands cap-blocked. Consolidating an existing endpoint into another file via method dispatch, or into `vercel.json` `rewrites` via a `?task=` parameter, is preferred over adding a new file. Both rules are enforced by `scripts/check_api_routes.py`, wired into `.pre-commit-config.yaml` as a local pre-commit hook so a PR cannot reintroduce a collision or push the count past eleven without the check going red. The check also runs standalone.

    Alternatives Considered

    - Trust Vercel to fail the build on collision. Rejected: the current builder emits both functions with no error, and the failing route is only visible at request time on the deployed URL. The team has no way to force this behaviour and no signal that it will change. - Rename every colliding file to a distinct URL (for example `api/events/index.ts` becomes `api/events/list.ts` serving `/api/events/list`). Rejected: it fragments a single logical resource across two URLs, requires every caller and every route mock in the E2E suite to be updated, and does not address the twelve-function cap. It also concedes the URL contract to a routing quirk rather than the resource model. - Move all multi-verb dispatch into `vercel.json` `rewrites` (the pattern already used for `/api/auth/verify` and `/api/cron/notification-worker`). Rejected as the default: adding a `rewrites` entry per endpoint balloons the config and hides routing behaviour in a file separate from the handler. Rewrites remain the right tool when the same handler serves several logical task names (as with the cron dispatcher); method dispatch inside one file is the right tool when the URL is the same and only the verb changes. - Split the backend out of Vercel serverless entirely and run it on a single long-lived container (Fly, Railway, or a small Node process on Supabase edge). Rejected for release 1: the free-tier deploy story on Vercel plus Supabase is deliberately what the team chose, and the cost of the collision was one dead endpoint that a hook can prevent, not a systemic runtime problem.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    📄 View ADR-014-one-file-per-vercel-serverless-api-route.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-015

    Cookie sessions everywhere; no Supabase Auth in Release 1

    Accepted
    Related BDR: T-58

    Context

    Two authentication mechanisms shipped in parallel during Sprint 1 and never interoperated: - **Cookie sessions.** `POST /api/auth/session` validates email and password, issues a random 32-byte token, and sets it as `cs_access` (HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, 1 hour). Stored as a sha256 hash in `auth_sessions`. Includes lockout at 5 failed attempts (SCRUM-94), full E14-S02 audit trail, and the E01-EXT email verification token flow (SCRUM-93). Implemented in `backend/src/modules/accessControl/sessions.ts` and consumed via `currentUser(request)` in `backend/src/modules/eventVisibility/runtime.ts`. - **Supabase Auth bearer tokens.** `backend/src/auth/supabase.ts` used `@supabase/supabase-js` to validate an inbound JWT and look the user up in the local `users` table. Consumed only in `api/events.ts` for POST/PATCH/ DELETE/GET-mine. The two paths did not interoperate. A user who logged in through `/api/auth/session` had a cookie but no Supabase JWT; a request to `POST /api/events` returned 401 because the events endpoint had no idea what the cookie meant. `App.tsx` papered over this by hard-coding `getAccessToken = async () => 'mock-token'` on the organiser routes, which turned the whole submit-event-request path into a static demo. SCRUM-90 as originally written was to "integrate Supabase Auth for login session handling", i.e. to make the Supabase Auth path the real one. That duplicated the cookie work already shipped (SCRUM-16 login, SCRUM-93 verification, SCRUM-94 lockout), would have discarded the audit-log and lockout state machines built on top of the cookie session table, and would have added a JWT verification layer that a single-tenant SPA does not need.

    Decision

    Release 1 uses one authentication mechanism: **cookie sessions**. Every authenticated request goes through the `currentUser(request)` lookup that validates the `cs_access` cookie against the `auth_sessions` table. Every endpoint that today calls `getAuthenticatedAppUser(bearerToken)` moves to `currentUser(request)` plus a role check. Frontend consequences: - No component takes a `getAccessToken` callback prop any more. - Every `fetch()` to a same-origin `/api/*` endpoint sends the session cookie automatically because the request is same-origin; no `credentials: 'include'` is required. For belt-and-braces we set `credentials: 'same-origin'` explicitly. - Prototype and offline-simulation modes (the `/prototype` route) distinguish themselves with an explicit `prototype` prop rather than by passing a null access token. Backend consequences: - `backend/src/auth/supabase.ts` is deleted. - The server-side `@supabase/supabase-js` dependency is removed if no server code reads it. The frontend Vite build continues to consume the browser-side Supabase client for Supabase Storage or realtime if those features arrive later; that is a different concern from auth. - The Vercel env vars `SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` (server) can be removed if the server no longer reads it. `PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` / `PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` and their `VITE_*` mirrors stay for the frontend.

    Alternatives Considered

    - **Migrate everything to Supabase Auth**, i.e. what SCRUM-90 originally named. Rejected. Loses SCRUM-94 lockout on the cookie session table, discards the E14-S02 audit-log integration already wired to cookie session lifecycle, and re-implements SCRUM-93 email verification through Supabase's separate confirm-email flow. Costs the whole Sprint 1 access-identity vertical to gain a JWT layer this app does not need. - **Run both auth systems** and expose the difference as two API paths (cookie for old, JWT for new). Rejected: this is the state Sprint 1 ended in and the reason the SCRUM-42 route collision was so hard to notice. Two auth systems means every future story asks which one to use. - **Introduce a session-to-JWT bridge**, i.e. after cookie login the server mints a Supabase JWT the frontend can send back. Rejected as over-engineering: it reintroduces the JWT surface area we don't need and forces the same audit-log and lockout work to duplicate across two representations.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    📄 View ADR-015-cookie-sessions-not-supabase-auth.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-016

    Thirty-minute login lockout after five failures

    Accepted
    Related BDR: C-30 T-38 O-02

    Context

    E01-S01 requires an account to be locked after five consecutive incorrect passwords, guidance on resetting the password, recovery through an emailed reset link, and an activity-log entry. BDR T-38 and O-02 established the threshold and reset-link recovery but did not specify a timed lock duration. The existing implementation in `backend/src/modules/accessControl/sessions.ts` uses a 30-minute lock. This record documents the team's confirmation on 18 September 2026 that this duration and automatic expiry are the intended policy. It is a team decision, not a customer-specified duration.

    Decision

    - The fifth consecutive incorrect password for an active, unlocked account sets `failed_login_count` to five and `locked_until` to 30 minutes after that failure, using the database clock. - During this period, login is refused even with the correct password. Further attempts do not extend the deadline or create additional lockout audit entries. - On the first login attempt at or after `locked_until`, clear the expired lock and reset the failure count before checking that attempt. Expiry permits another attempt; it does not authenticate the user or reactivate an inactive account. - A successful login before the fifth failure resets the consecutive count. - Password reset remains an alternative recovery path before the 30 minutes have elapsed. A successful reset clears the lock and failure count and permits login with the new password. - Reset links expire 15 minutes after issuance and are single-use. This is separate from the 30-minute account lock duration. - Record one `Account Locked` activity-log entry when the fifth failure triggers the lock. Update the account and audit log in the same transaction, serializing attempts for the same account. - Keep failed-login responses generic and provide password-reset guidance without revealing whether an email address is registered.

    Alternatives Considered

    - Lock until a successful password reset, with no automatic expiry. Rejected in favour of a bounded waiting period while retaining reset-based recovery. - Extend the lock on every subsequent attempt. Rejected because repeated attempts could keep another user's account locked indefinitely.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    📄 View ADR-016-thirty-minute-login-lockout.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-017

    Story owners build their own frontend on a shared skeleton

    Accepted
    Related BDR: None

    Context

    ADR-007 settled on one single-page application for all five roles. It did not settle who builds each screen, or how they are kept consistent. Through Sprint 1 and most of Sprint 2 the team worked to a split recorded in `.agents/STATE.md` on 26 September 2026: one developer (Amareet) built all frontend work, and the other five built backends. Screens that pre-dated that split were built by whoever owned the story, each in their own style. By the end of Sprint 2 two problems were visible: - **One frontend developer was a bottleneck.** Every story's screen queued behind that person once its backend landed, while five developers produced backends in parallel. Sprint 1 delivered about 24 of 36 planned points, and Sprint 2 was tracking at a similar rate, with 25 stories (83 points) still planned for Sprints 3 and 4. - **The frontend had no common design language.** The code on `main` has 13 feature-specific page wrappers and 9 heading styles beside the shared `.page-heading`. `.eyebrow` is redefined in 8 stylesheets and `.primary-action` in 4. There are about 20 raw font sizes next to a five-step type scale, and six corner radii. The Organiser event list and the venue search screen use almost none of the shared styles. After a team discussion on 30 September 2026, the course instructor gave feedback that the team needed a common design language as a high priority and that a single frontend developer was too great a bottleneck.

    Decision

    - **Each story's owner builds that story's frontend as well as its backend.** The owner is the Jira assignee. This applies from Sprint 3 onward, and to any Sprint 2 story whose frontend is not yet started. - **Owners build on a shared frontend skeleton**, delivered under SCRUM-116 and owned by Amareet: - an app shell (shared header and page frame) on every route; - a single route list that drives routing, role navigation and the per-role login redirect; - design tokens (colour, type scale, spacing and radius); - about a dozen shared building blocks, including page heading, card, buttons, form field, status pill, data list, alert, and the loading, empty, error and refused states; - four page templates: List, Detail, Form and Decision; - a standard data-loading pattern that ignores late responses; - test helpers and a short developer guide. - **A design-language document, `design.md` (SCRUM-117, owned by Bryan), sets the rules** that the skeleton implements. Where the two disagree, the difference is raised and resolved rather than chosen silently. - **The skeleton is delivered in small PRs, not as a single restyle.** Existing pages move onto it when their owner next changes them. Amareet moves their own Sprint 2 pages across (SCRUM-119) as the working reference. - **Le Xin's E05-S04 maintenance-blocks screen (SCRUM-120) is the pilot**, to test the skeleton before other owners adopt it. - **The previous split is retired.** Amareet remains Scrum Master and owns the skeleton, and reviews and pairs on other owners' frontend work instead of building every screen.

    Alternatives Considered

    - **Keep a single frontend developer.** Rejected: it is the bottleneck the instructor identified, and the backlog cannot be delivered at that pace. - **Let each owner build screens with no shared skeleton.** Rejected: it is how the current inconsistencies arose, and it contradicts the instructor's call for a common design language. - **Build every screen in the frontend first, then hand them over for backend wiring.** Rejected: it keeps the same bottleneck and duplicates effort, because most Sprint 3 and 4 screens already exist as mock screens that only need connecting to real data. - **Adopt a third-party component library.** Not chosen for now. The existing tokens and components cover the needs identified in the screen inventory, and a new dependency would add learning and migration work. It can be revisited in `design.md`.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    📄 View ADR-017-story-owners-build-their-frontend-on-a-shared-skeleton.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-018

    Restore Sessions as first-class Event entities

    Accepted — team decision recorded 13 October 2026
    Related BDR: C-62 C-107 T-48 T-79 T-85 T-98 T-99 O-10 O-50 O-51

    Context

    Week 4 C-62 led the team to represent each programme session as a separate Event (T-48), so ADR-004 and ADR-005 were retired. Week 9 C-107 now describes venue bookings across separate Session periods, including repeat bookings of one Venue, and equipment reservations for the specific Session timing and Venue. The team selected T-79 to restore Session as a child of Event while retaining C-62 as the historical answer that informed the earlier decision.

    Decision

    An Event contains one or more Sessions. Each Session owns its period, expected attendance, venue/layout/accessibility requirements, and equipment requirements. The Event's expected-attendance value remains the overall planning total; it is not a booking-suitability fallback or registration cap. Venue bookings and equipment requests/reservations reference a Session. Store both `session_id` and `event_id` on dependent rows and enforce their ownership with a composite foreign key. Event status and lifecycle, registration windows, and technical-support requests/assignments remain Event-level. An attendee has one active registration per Event and selects one or more Sessions in that registration. Per-Session and combined Event capacity are enforced as recorded in T-85. T-98 closes O-50: the Event-level waitlist remains available for combined Event capacity, with no per-Session waitlist. T-99 closes O-51: copying an Event copies its requirements and Session structure, clears dates/times, and omits bookings, equipment reservations and registrations.

    Alternatives Considered

    - Keep the Week 4 one-Event-per-Session model from C-62/T-48. Not selected for Release 1 after the team adopted the later C-107 answer in T-79. - Move registration windows and event lifecycle to each Session. Not selected; T-79 and T-85 keep registration and lifecycle at Event level. - Attach only equipment to Sessions while leaving venue bookings at Event level. Not selected; T-79 links both venue bookings and equipment requests/reservations to a Session.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    - The schema and shared API contracts need Session ownership constraints. A booking period and suitability fallback use the linked Session; the Event's overall attendance remains separate planning context; technical support remains Event-wide. - Event registration stores selected Sessions in a join table. Capacity checks must atomically enforce each selected Session and the combined capacity derived from confirmed Session layouts. - Existing Event dates and requirements need a data-preserving backfill into one Session per Event. Existing registrations select that Session; existing venue and equipment rows link to it. Keep audit history and Event-level lifecycle/support data intact. - Existing references to the retired model remain historical. Do not rewrite C-62 or claim that the Week 4 answer was erroneous.

    📄 View ADR-018-restoring-sessions-as-first-class-event-entities.md on GitHub ↗
    ADR-019

    Allow multiple roles per account

    Accepted — team decision recorded 13 October 2026
    Related BDR: C-136 T-10 T-72 T-86 O-44

    Context

    ADR-012 represented a user with one `USERS.role` value. Week 9 C-136 confirms that accounts are preloaded and users do not self-register; it does not define role cardinality. The team selected T-86 to allow one account to hold multiple roles while keeping the initial seed data simple.

    Decision

    Role membership is many-to-many: an account may hold multiple system roles. Seed data assigns exactly one role to each account. Authorization continues to check the authenticated account's granted roles for every API request; one-role seed data is not a product constraint. The precise UI treatment for an account with multiple roles is an implementation/design detail and must not reduce its authorized access.

    Alternatives Considered

    - Keep exactly one role in `USERS.role` for Release 1. Superseded by T-86. - Create one account per role. Rejected in ADR-012 because it fragments one person's identity and audit trail.

    What It Buys Us

    What It Costs Us / Consequences

    - Replace the single role column with a `USER_ROLES` membership relation and migrate every existing role value into one membership row before removing the old column. - Update authentication/session claims, backend authorization guards, frontend navigation, role setup and access-control tests to consume role memberships. - Keep seed fixtures at one membership per user until a story needs to exercise multiple roles; add explicit multi-role coverage then. - Do not infer that a user can switch roles through a dedicated screen. The interface must expose only actions allowed by the account's assigned roles; any role-context selector needs design review.

    📄 View ADR-019-multiple-roles-per-account.md on GitHub ↗

    T-56 Team Decision

    One file per Vercel serverless API route, function count held at 11

    Vercel's file-based routing collapses `api/foo.ts` and `api/foo/index.ts` onto the same URL, and the build ships both lambdas without a warning. One silently wins the route; the other is an unreachable slot against the Hobby plan's twelve-function cap. PR #56 (SCRUM-26) added `api/events.ts` next to the pre-existing `api/events/index.ts` from PR #42 (SCRUM-18 hide internal planning info from Attendees, story E01-S03), which made `GET /api/events` return 405 in production for the whole of Sprint 1 and left the organiser browse-events screen backed by ClientEvents.tsx broken without anyone noticing. Adopting one file per URL with method dispatch inside the file eliminates the collision and returns a lambda slot; capping the file count at 11 keeps one slot of headroom so the next story does not land cap-blocked. Enforced by `scripts/check_api_routes.py` as a pre-commit hook and by `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. See ADR-014. Postplan documenting the discovery: <https://4ovp804r75sa.postplan.dev> (v1 misattributed the visibility work to SCRUM-42; correct mapping is SCRUM-18 per `docs/jira-sprint-setup.md`).

    Affects: api/events.ts, api/events/index.ts (deleted), backend/tests/eventVisibility.integration.test.ts, .pre-commit-config.yaml, scripts/check_api_routes.py, docs/adr/ADR-014-one-file-per-vercel-serverless-api-route.md, docs/plans/sprint-1-retrospective.md, docs/deploying-and-debugging.md

Making all ten skippable would need a migration relaxing those three constraints, with ripple effects on other modules (`venueBooking`, notifications, audit logs) that may assume every event row has a title, dates and an attendance figure — disproportionate for a 3-point story. Team decision: title, dates and expected attendance stay mandatory for a draft too, validated the same way as a full submission; the other seven skip the missing-field check while `status = 'draft'`. No migration. Confirmed by Aaron on 2026-09-18.

    T-58 Team Decision

    Cookie sessions everywhere; delete the parallel Supabase Auth wiring

    Sprint 1 shipped two authentication mechanisms alongside each other: custom cookie sessions (api/auth/session.ts + backend/src/modules/accessControl/sessions.ts) covering login, lockout, verification, and audit-log integration for E01, plus a parallel Supabase Auth bearer-token path in backend/src/auth/supabase.ts that api/events.ts used for organiser create/edit/delete. The two paths did not interoperate. A user who logged in through /api/auth/session had a cookie but no Supabase JWT, so POST /api/events returned 401. App.tsx papered over this by hard-coding `getAccessToken = async () => 'mock-token'`. Team decision: cookie sessions everywhere in Release 1. api/events.ts moves to the same currentUser() lookup the whoami endpoint uses. backend/src/auth/supabase.ts and the server-side @supabase/supabase-js dependency are deleted. Frontend components drop the getAccessToken prop; every fetch uses `credentials: 'same-origin'`. The /prototype route takes an explicit `prototype` prop to opt out of live fetch instead of passing a null access token. See ADR-015. Confirmed by Bryan on 2026-09-17.

    Affects: api/events.ts, backend/src/auth/supabase.ts (deleted), App.tsx, OrganiserRequestFlow, OrganiserDrafts
    Follows / Supersedes: ADR-015
    T-59 Team Decision

    Use a `test` schema in the same Supabase DB instead of a separate test project

    SCRUM-109 originally provisioned a second Supabase project for `TEST_DATABASE_URL`. That consumes a Supabase free-tier slot on Bryan's account and adds a second DB URL to rotate for every integration test we add. Team decision: create a `test` schema inside the existing sgconnectsphere Supabase project and mirror every `public.<table>` under `test.<table>`. PostgreSQL enforces the schema boundary at the storage layer, so `TRUNCATE test.users` cannot touch `public.users` and no test SQL can accidentally see prod rows. Tests connect with `SET search_path = test, public;`. RLS policies are one-per-schema (small extra config). Rejected alternatives: (a) prod tables with a `test_` row prefix, which leaves TRUNCATE dangerous, (b) prod tables with a JSON `is_test = true` column, which leaves every query at risk of forgetting the filter. Confirmed by Bryan on 2026-09-18.

    T-65 Team Decision

    Record a test run in `docs/testing/runs/` whenever the run is used as evidence

    The team had no execution log: the test-case catalogue in `docs/testing/cases/` says what should be tested, but nothing recorded who ran what, when, against which commit, or with what outcome. The course deliverable needs that ledger in Excel at project end. Decision: one Markdown file per run session under `docs/testing/runs/`, named `YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS-<github-username>-<scope>.md`, carrying YAML frontmatter plus a table of TC_ID, test name, outcome and remarks.<br><br>Scope is deliberately narrow. A record is required only when a run is **used as evidence**: cited in a pull request, offered as proof that a story meets its Definition of Done, or shown in a demo. Exploratory runs during development need none, and CI runs are covered by their own immutable Actions log unless someone cites one. An earlier draft said every execution of every test command, which read literally covered every `npm test` while developing and every CI run, and nobody can commit those by hand.<br><br>Session-per-file rather than test-per-file: a file per test result would produce hundreds of files and a conflict whenever two people ran overlapping suites, whereas every session filename is unique by timestamp plus username, so no two people ever edit the same file and merge conflicts are impossible by construction. The `scope` field is a fixed enum so an agent cannot invent values and break the exporter. There is deliberately no BACKFILL outcome: historic runs reconstructed from PR evidence use the normal PASS or FAIL with the correct backdated date and cite their source in the remarks. Records are immutable once merged, so a later catalogue revision never rewrites history.<br><br>This does not replace the per-story traceability matrices (for example `docs/plans/scrum-33-implementation-status.md`), which remain required by the Traceability Standard in `docs/testing/README.md`. Those hold the narrative and the rule-to-test mapping; session records hold the flat exportable execution log. A story log should cite a session filename as well as restating the command, the result, and the exact message seen, so a later report can be matched against what testing saw.<br><br>Raised by Aaron in review of PR #166, who asked that a team-wide obligation be agreed rather than merged on one person's authority. Approved by Bryan on 2026-10-01.

    T-66 Team Decision

    Return E05-S05 to Release 1 with per-venue setup and turnaround buffers

    C-65 reverses C-18 and C-38, so the explicit customer exclusion that deferred E05-S05 no longer applies. Setup and turnaround are two whole-minute attributes of a venue, set by Venue Staff on the venue record; E05-S01 is Done, so the configure scenario belongs to E05-S05 rather than being added to E05-S01 (T-74). They default to 0 for every existing venue so no data migration changes current availability on its own. A booking's occupancy window is [start minus setup, end plus turnaround]; every availability display and conflict check uses that window instead of the advertised start and end. E05-S03 (calendar) and E06-S01 (search) are Done, so the buffered calendar display and the buffered search are scenarios of E05-S05; E06-S03, E06-S04, E06-S05 and E06-S06 are not started and gain a buffer scenario each in place (T-74). Tentative holds occupy the venue, so they carry the buffers too. Maintenance blocks are a property of the venue itself and are not buffered (O-22). When a buffer is created or changed and an existing booking now overlaps, the booking is flagged as Conflicting and left in place; nothing is released automatically, matching the customer's "identified rather than silently removed". Who sees the flag and whether the save is allowed are O-20 and O-21; the story is written to the defaults recorded there. ADR-003's exclusion constraint must operate on the buffered range, which is the architecture PR's job.

    Affects: E05-S05, E05-S01, E05-S03, E06-S01, E06-S03, E06-S04, E06-S05, E06-S06, ADR-003

    T-67 Team Decision

    Deliver Change 2 as a new E05 story that withdraws E05-S04's refusal of blocks over confirmed bookings, and return E10-S05 to Release 1

    E05-S04 is in the Sprint 2 sprint backlog (backend merged in #151, frontend in review), and the Week 3 rule is that stories are fixed for the duration of a sprint. Its acceptance criteria are therefore not edited now. C-66 contradicts one of them: E05-S04 refuses a block that overlaps a confirmed booking, whereas the customer says unavailability "may occur even when future events have already been booked" and the bookings should be "identified". The delta is delivered as a new story in E05 (ID assigned in the backlog PR): Venue Staff may mark a venue unavailable for a period with a reason category (maintenance, equipment failure, renovation, safety concern, other); overlapping pending and confirmed bookings become Conflicting; the event is never cancelled or moved automatically, consistent with C-48, C-61 and T-28; the Coordinator is notified through the existing E11-S01 "Venue blocked" row and may search for and request a replacement through E06-S01 and E06-S03. E10-S05 (handle a venue lost from a confirmed event) returns to Release 1 because the "preserve the original event information while allowing the coordinator to search for and request a replacement venue" sentence is that story. Whether unavailability may be open-ended, what a Confirmed event's status does, who else is told, and whether a booking is restored when the venue reopens are O-23 to O-26, written to their defaults.

    Affects: E05-S04 (unchanged this sprint), new E05 story, E10-S05, E06-S01, E06-S03, E11-S01

    T-68 Team Decision

    Retire T-20 and allow several venue bookings per event, each checked independently

    C-67 requires one event to hold more than one venue booking. T-20 ("one pending venue request per session at a time") and E06-S03 Scenario 3, which blocks a second pending request for the same event, are the direct contradiction and are retired. The customer's own example, an auditorium plus three breakout rooms, cannot be booked sensibly if each request must be decided before the next is raised, so several pending requests at once are allowed. Each booking is checked on its own against its venue's availability and conflicts, including the T-66 buffers; the C-60 one-hold-per-venue-slot rule is unaffected because it constrains a venue, not an event. The first booking request still moves the event to Planning. Cancelling or changing one booking never removes another; the Coordinator may explicitly cancel the rest. E08-S03's "a confirmed venue booking" becomes "every venue booking confirmed or withdrawn" by default (O-28). E10-S02's arrangement-impact check applies to every booking. How suitability is judged when breakout rooms are smaller than the event's expected attendance (O-27), whether bookings may have differing time windows (O-29) and which venue Attendees are shown (O-30) are open and written to their defaults.

    Amend T-49: every tentative hold carries an expiry and is expired by the system

    C-68 reverses the "no expiry figure has been invented" position in T-49, C-01, C-16 and C-60. E06-S05 gains an expiry date and time on every hold. A scheduled job, running on the existing outbox and relay worker rather than a new scheduler, releases expired holds so the slot shows Free on the calendar (E05-S03) and can be requested by others; an expired hold is never counted as confirmed anywhere, including the E08-S03 confirmation gate. The Coordinator is notified before and at expiry through two new E11-S01 rows. Who sets the expiry and the default (O-31), the action that stops expiry (O-32), reminder timing (O-33) and extension (O-34) are open; the story is written to the defaults recorded there.

    T-70 Team Decision

    Retire T-14 and rewrite E03-S01 around an unassigned queue worked by the Event Coordinator Lead

    C-69 states that new requests are "no longer assigned directly to an Event Coordinator". That removes the premise of T-14, so auto-assignment is retired rather than kept as a fallback; a fallback would contradict the customer's sentence. E03-S01 is Done (#141, #147) and stays Done (T-74, guide Scenario 2): its auto-assignment scenarios are marked superseded in the backlog, not deleted or rewritten, and its delivered points are untouched. The new behaviour is new E03 stories: on submission an event enters an unassigned queue visible to the Lead; the Lead reviews basic event information, assigns a Coordinator, and the event moves to Under Review; the Lead may reassign at any time. The existing Coordinator-initiated reassignment with acceptance (T-15, C-56) is kept, so T-15 is amended to add the Lead as a second actor rather than replaced. Coordinators see and manage only events assigned to them; E01-S02 is Done, so that is a new E01 story rather than an edit to E01-S02. The Lead sees every assignment and active event. Assignment and reassignment notify the incoming Coordinator, the outgoing Coordinator where there is one, and the Organiser, through E11-S01. Whether there is one Lead or several (O-35), whether a Lead reassignment needs acceptance (O-36), whether Coordinators may still request reassignment (O-37) and whether Coordinators can see the queue (O-38) are open; the story is written to the defaults recorded there. The backlog PR adds the Lead's queue, reassignment and oversight stories in E03 and the Coordinator-visibility story in E01.

    T-71 Team Decision

    Add a Safety Review gate between Planning and Confirmed as the interim placement of C-70's Operational Safety Check

    C-70 says the check happens "after the venue and technical arrangements have been confirmed" and "before the event can proceed to preparation". In the canonical model the moment all arrangements are confirmed is exactly the E08-S03 Confirm gate, and nothing after Confirmed is called preparation. The team's reading is therefore that Confirmed is the state in which preparation may begin, and the safety check sits immediately before it. A new status, Safety Review, is inserted: Planning → Safety Review (the Coordinator submits for review once every arrangement is confirmed) → Confirmed (approved) or Planning (rejected or changes requested, with a mandatory reason and the items to revisit). Neither rejection nor a change request cancels the event. The Safety Officer records a decision against the factors the customer listed; the decision and reason are written to the activity log (E14-S02, ADR-009) and notified to the Coordinator and Organiser through E11-S01. The customer guarantees a response, so no timeout path is built. This placement is interim and is the first question for the Q&A (O-39); if the customer places preparation after Confirmed instead, the status model gains a stage after Confirmed and E08-S05 moves accordingly. Trigger (O-40), reject versus request-changes semantics (O-41), checklist shape (O-42) and retroactive application (O-43) are open and written to their defaults. New stories for the Safety Officer's review screen and the Coordinator's submit-for-review step are added in the backlog PR.

    Affects: Canonical status model, E08-S03, E08-S04, E03-S05, E01-S11, E14-S02, E11-S01, new E08 stories
    Follows / Supersedes: C-70

ADR-007 ("one single-page application for all five roles") and ADR-012 are amended in the architecture PR, and both roles gain a route and home screen on the shared skeleton (ADR-017) through a new E01 story, because E01-S01 (log in) is Done and is not reopened for a new requirement (T-74). This is recorded once here so the two role additions share one migration and one set of ADR amendments rather than two.

    T-73 Team Decision

    Write the Week 7 stories now against recorded defaults and amend after the customer Q&A, rather than waiting

    The Week 7 document is final ("the customer does not anticipate any further changes for Release 1") and must be implemented in full, but the customer Q&A that would resolve its ambiguities may be a week or more away, after Sprint 3 planning on 5 October 2026. The Week 2 rule is that a story is negotiable until the sprint it is pulled into starts. The team therefore writes every affected story now; each ambiguity is an entry in section C (O-20 to O-44) carrying the default the story is written to; every acceptance-criterion line that depends on one is tagged "(assumes O-xx)". Sprint 3 planning pulls first the stories whose criteria carry no High-priority open item. When the Q&A answers arrive, the affected criteria are amended and the open item closed before that story is pulled into a sprint; a story already in a sprint keeps its default to the end of that sprint and the correction is a follow-up. Changes 1, 4 and 5 are mostly inferable from the document and are expected to be Sprint 3 work; parts of Changes 2, 3 and 6 each hinge on one High-priority item. Estimation follows the Week 7 guide step 4: new stories are estimated by planning poker at Sprint 3 planning; a To Do story whose scenarios changed is re-estimated only if the change materially alters its size (E06-S03 and E08-S03 probably do, E06-S05 probably does); a Done story is never re-estimated; an in-flight story (E05-S04) is estimated for its remaining work only.

    Affects: Sprint 3 and Sprint 4 planning, section C
    Follows / Supersedes: C-65 to C-70, Week 2 slide 29, Week 3 slide 57, Week 7 guide steps 1 and 4
    T-74 Team Decision

    A Done story stays Done; new behaviour that touches it is a new story; an incomplete story is updated in place; a story is reopened only when one of its original criteria turns out unsatisfied

    The Week 7 guide ("Managing Changes", Scenarios 1 to 3) sets the rule: a new requirement never reopens a Done story, it becomes a new story with its own criteria and estimate, and the Done story keeps its points so velocity history stays honest; a Done story is reopened, and only its remaining work estimated, when an original criterion was missed or implemented wrongly; an incomplete story simply has its criteria updated. Applied to the Week 7 changes: E03-S01, E05-S01, E05-S03, E06-S01, E03-S05, E01-S01, E01-S02 and E01-S11 are Done and stay Done, with any superseded scenario marked "Superseded by Exx-Sxx (C-nn)" in the backlog rather than deleted and any new behaviour placed in a new story (E06-S01's buffered search in E05-S05; E03-S05's and E01-S11's Safety Review handling in E08-S06); E06-S03, E06-S05, E06-S06, E08-S03, E08-S04, E10-S02 and E11-S01 are not Done and are updated in place; E05-S04 is in the Sprint 2 sprint backlog and is neither edited nor reopened, its correction being the new story under T-67. No Week 7 change is a Scenario 1 or 3 reopening: no original criterion has been found unsatisfied. When a Done story's original criteria could be affected by a new story (E03-S01's status transition, E05-S03's calendar states, E01-S02's Organiser isolation), the new story's test cases include a regression case asserting the original behaviour still holds, per guide step 3.

    Affects: Every Week 7 backlog PR; Sprint 3 planning; Jira (no Done story is reopened)
